questions.subtopic: 2A3 Planning around key risks and controls. An installment left in long-term debt
questions.question: Planning assurance on an Ecuadorian bottler's loan covenant, a current ratio of at least 1.2, auditor Ximena sees 1.25 reported; a loan's installment due in four months sits within long-term debt. Which conclusion is BEST?

options.A: The 1.25 ratio stands, since long-term debt falls outside the current ratio
options.B: Total liabilities are understated by the installment's amount
options.C: Owners' equity is overstated by the installment's amount
options.D: The 1.25 ratio overstates compliance; current liabilities omit the installment

questions.key_concept: The part of a long-term loan due within the year is a current liability; leaving it in long-term debt makes the current ratio look stronger.
questions.pre_read: Recall where the part of a long-term loan due within the year belongs on the balance sheet, and what the current ratio compares.
questions.correct_explanation: OpenStax's accounting text classes the part of a long-term note due within the year as a current liability, and the SEC's balance sheet captions, for example, list the current portion of long-term debt among current liabilities. Left in long-term debt, the installment drops out of the current ratio's denominator, so 1.25 may overstate compliance with a 1.2 covenant. Option A treats the whole loan as long-term; Standard 13.2 has Ximena plan around this risk.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the loan is long-term, but its installment due within the year is a current liability, so where it sits does change the current ratio.
wrong_explanations.B: Total liabilities stay the same whichever line holds the installment; the misclassification moves it between current and long-term debt without leaving it out.
wrong_explanations.C: The installment is owed to the lender, so it is a liability, not owners' equity; equity changes only where a liability is wrongly recorded as capital.

tips: Eliminate: B, because moving the installment between lines leaves total liabilities unchanged, and C, because a lender's loan is a liability, not owners' equity.
Final two: D beats A because an installment due within the year is a current liability; leaving it in long-term debt lifts the current ratio above its true level.
Exam cue: on CIA planning questions about the balance sheet, ask when each item falls due or turns to cash; within the year means current.

questions.subtopic: 2A3 Planning around key risks and controls. Bonds held for years in a funds report
questions.question: Planning an engagement on whether an Ethiopian coffee cooperative can meet next harvest's payments, auditor Selam sees its available-funds report includes listed bonds the board resolved to hold five years. Which conclusion is BEST?

options.A: Funds may be fairly stated, as listed bonds sell readily for cash
options.B: Funds may be overstated, as bonds the cooperative holds count as debt
options.C: Funds may be overstated, as the bonds are long-term investments
options.D: Funds may be fairly stated, if bonds are shown at market value

questions.key_concept: An investment management intends to hold beyond a year is a long-term investment, not a current asset, however readily it could be sold.
questions.pre_read: Recall what makes an asset current, and whether an investment's class turns on how easily it sells or how long management means to hold it.
questions.correct_explanation: OpenStax's accounting text treats a current asset as one turned into cash or used within a year or operating cycle, and a long-term investment as stocks or bonds management intends to hold for longer. Bonds the board resolved to keep five years are long-term investments, so counting them as available funds may overstate cash for next harvest's payments. Option A looks at how easily bonds sell, but intent to hold, not marketability, decides their class.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: listed bonds may trade readily, but the board's resolution to hold them five years makes them long-term investments, so they do not fund next harvest's payments.
wrong_explanations.B: Bonds the cooperative holds are an investment it owns; bonds it had issued would be debt, and the stem describes none.
wrong_explanations.D: Market value changes what the bonds are worth, not when they turn to cash; held for five years, they still fall outside funds for next harvest.

tips: Eliminate: B, because bonds the cooperative holds are an asset, not borrowing, and D, because valuing the bonds at market does not bring them within the year.
Final two: C beats A because intent decides: bonds the board will hold five years are long-term investments, not current assets, however easily they could be sold.
Exam cue: on CIA questions about assets, ask whether the item turns to cash within the year; for investments, management's intent to hold, not how easily they sell, decides.

questions.subtopic: 2A3 Planning around key risks and controls. Real-time stock records without a count
questions.question: Planning an inventory engagement at a Tunisian phone distributor, auditor Amira hears that a new ERP system keeps perpetual stock records, so management dropped the yearly count. Which risk MOST needs rating?

options.A: Sold phones may stay in recorded stock until a year-end posting
options.B: Stolen or damaged phones may stay in recorded stock balances
options.C: Deliveries may be paid before the warehouse records their receipt
options.D: Counting may cost more than the stock differences it would reveal

questions.key_concept: A perpetual inventory system updates with each transaction but records no theft, damage or loss; only a physical count compares records with stock on hand.
questions.pre_read: Recall what a perpetual inventory system updates and when, and whether it removes the need for a physical count.
questions.correct_explanation: OpenStax's accounting text notes that a perpetual system updates inventory with each purchase and sale yet still needs a periodic physical count, because shrinkage, damage and obsolescence leave records and shelves apart. With the count dropped, nothing would reveal phones that vanished without a transaction, so Standard 13.2 has Amira rate that risk. Option A describes a periodic system, which updates stock only at period end.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: posting stock at period end describes a periodic system; a perpetual system updates with each sale, so the gap it leaves is loss with no transaction.
wrong_explanations.C: Paying before receipt is recorded is a purchasing risk where receiving and paying are not matched, but the stem's change concerns the dropped count.
wrong_explanations.D: Cost against benefit is a fair test, but the benefit cannot be judged while the records go unchecked; losses without a transaction show up only in a count.

tips: Eliminate: C, because the stem's change is the dropped count, not purchasing, and D, because the size of stock differences stays unknown until a count is made.
Final two: B beats A because a perpetual system posts each sale as it happens, yet cannot record phones that disappear without a transaction; only a count finds them.
Exam cue: on CIA planning questions, a system that records every transaction is not proof that assets exist; look for a physical check against the records.

questions.subtopic: 2A4 Choosing the engagement approach. A subject redesigned every month
questions.question: Supervisor Inês plans assurance on intake controls at a Portuguese hospital opening in five months; management redesigns intake after each monthly staff trial, and the approved objective needs assurance before opening. Which approach is BEST?

options.A: Monthly cycles, one per redesign, each program approved first
options.B: One approved program, testing intake once the hospital has opened
options.C: One approved program, fixed now on this month's intake design
options.D: Advisory input on each redesign, under an approved engagement plan

questions.key_concept: Short audit cycles suit a subject that keeps changing under a deadline, but each cycle's work program is still approved before it runs.
questions.pre_read: Recall when an adaptive, cycle-based approach fits better than a plan fixed at the start, and what Standard 13.6 requires of any work program.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 13.6 needs a work program that can achieve the engagement objectives, approved by the chief audit executive before it runs. OpenStax's information systems text describes an adaptive approach as repeating short planning cycles to absorb changing requirements, while a predictive plan suits fixed, well-defined goals. Intake changes monthly and assurance is due before opening, so cycles matched to each redesign fit, each program approved first. Option C would test a design about to change.

wrong_explanations.B: Testing after opening suits an objective about the running process; this objective needs assurance before opening, so it misses the time frame.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: a plan fixed at the start suits a stable subject, but intake changes monthly, so tests built on this month's design would not cover what opens.
wrong_explanations.D: Advice on each redesign suits a request for help shaping intake; the approved objective needs assurance before opening, which advisory input does not give.

tips: Eliminate: B, because testing after opening misses an objective that needs assurance before it, and D, because advice on each redesign gives no assurance.
Final two: A beats C because a plan fixed now would test a design that changes monthly; short cycles absorb each redesign, each program approved first.
Exam cue: on CIA approach questions, fit the approach to how settled the subject is and when results are due; agile changes timing, never the approval rule.

questions.subtopic: 2A6 Procedures and the work program. Showing how a lockout setting behaves
questions.question: In a Malaysian bank's IT systems engagement, auditor Farid must find whether online banking accounts lock after five failed sign-ins, as the security policy requires. Which method shows that MOST directly?

options.A: Review the system's list of accounts locked during the past month
options.B: Interview the security administrator on how lockouts are configured
options.C: Inspect the lockout setting against the security policy
options.D: Try repeated wrong passwords on a test account, noting the result

questions.key_concept: Exercising a control under set conditions and comparing the result with what should happen tests behavior; inspecting its setting shows only its configuration.
questions.pre_read: Recall the difference between examining a setting or record, interviewing staff, and testing a mechanism by making it act.
questions.correct_explanation: NIST SP 800-53A separates three assessment methods: examine (inspect or review settings, records and documents), interview, and test, which exercises a mechanism under set conditions and compares actual with expected behavior. The objective is what accounts do after five failures, so entering wrong passwords on a test account shows it directly. Option C shows only the configured limit, not whether accounts actually lock. Standard 14.1 favors evidence Farid obtains first-hand.

wrong_explanations.A: A list of locked accounts shows lockouts happened, not after how many failures; it comes from the system under review, whose behavior is the question.
wrong_explanations.B: Interviews build understanding and clarify, but the administrator's account of the configuration says nothing about what the system does when tried.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: comparing the setting with the policy shows how the control is configured, not how it behaves; only exercising the control under set conditions shows whether accounts actually lock.

tips: Eliminate: A, because a list of locked accounts does not show after how many failures they locked, and B, because an interview gives understanding, not behavior.
Final two: D beats C because the objective is what accounts do; a test exercises the control, while inspecting the setting shows only how it is configured.
Exam cue: on CIA test-method questions, match the method to the objective: settings answer how a control is configured, a test answers how it behaves.

questions.question: Planning purchasing assurance at a Jamaican hotel group, auditor Andre finds an ERP buyer role can raise orders, record deliveries and release payments; the finance manager approves payments over $2,000. Which risk is GREATEST?

options.A: Supplier bank details could be changed to divert payments elsewhere
options.B: A buyer could split payments below $2,000 to avoid approval
options.C: A buyer could order extra goods, record them delivered and keep them
options.D: Invoices could be paid late, losing early-payment discounts

questions.key_concept: Ordering, receiving and paying belong with different people; an approval resting on records one person made cannot replace that separation.
questions.pre_read: Recall why purchasing splits ordering, receiving and paying among different people, and what a later payment approval can and cannot see.
questions.correct_explanation: OpenStax's accounting text keeps ordering, receiving and paying with different people, so no one can order goods, accept them and have them paid alone. This role does all three, and the finance manager approves on order and delivery records the same buyer made, so goods ordered and kept pass at any amount (Standard 13.2: fraud risks). Splitting payments, option B, only dodges an approval that cannot see this.

wrong_explanations.A: Diverted bank details are a payment risk where a role can edit supplier records; nothing in the stem gives this buyer role that right.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: split payments dodge an approval threshold, but dodging adds little here: the manager approves records the same buyer made, so goods ordered and kept pass at any amount.
wrong_explanations.D: Late payment loses discounts, an efficiency cost; the stem's concern is one role controlling a purchase from order to payment, a loss and fraud risk.

tips: Eliminate: A, because the stem gives the buyer role no rights over supplier records, and D, because lost discounts are an efficiency cost, not the control gap the stem describes.
Final two: C beats B because the finance manager approves on order and delivery records the same buyer made; splitting payments only dodges an approval that cannot see goods ordered and kept.
Exam cue: on CIA planning questions, a payment approval does not replace separated duties; ask whether one person can order, accept and pay for goods alone.

questions.subtopic: 2A3 Planning around key risks and controls. A recovery target longer than the tolerable downtime
questions.question: Auditor Aigerim, planning a Kazakh grain trader's continuity engagement, reads the business impact analysis allows settlements at most 24 hours' disruption; the settlement system's recovery time objective is 36 hours. Which risk MOST needs attention?

options.A: Settlements could stay down past their maximum tolerable downtime
options.B: Restores could take longer than the system's recovery time objective
options.C: Recovery spending could exceed what settlements' tolerance requires
options.D: Recovery could stall if the plan names no one to lead it

questions.key_concept: A system's recovery time objective must fit inside the downtime its process can bear; a looser target fails even when restores meet it.
questions.pre_read: Recall how a business impact analysis's tolerable downtime and a system's recovery time objective relate, and which one must be shorter.
questions.correct_explanation: NIST SP 800-34 defines the recovery time objective as the longest a system may stay down before harming the processes it supports, and normally sets it shorter than their maximum tolerable downtime, leaving time to catch up on work. A 36-hour target against the analysis's 24-hour limit leaves settlements down past that downtime even when recovery is on time. Option B tests restores against a target that is itself too loose.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: timed restores show whether 36 hours is met, but meeting it would still leave settlements stopped 12 hours past what the analysis allows.
wrong_explanations.C: A recovery time objective caps downtime, so a 36-hour target means slower recovery than the 24-hour tolerance, not spending beyond what settlements need.
wrong_explanations.D: A plan naming no recovery lead is a real gap where roles are unclear, but the stem gives no sign of it; the gap lies in the recovery target itself.

tips: Eliminate: C, because a longer recovery time objective means slower recovery, not extra spending, and D, because nothing suggests the plan lacks a recovery lead.
Final two: A beats B because a recovery target must sit inside the downtime the process can bear; restores that meet a 36-hour target still break a 24-hour limit.
Exam cue: on CIA continuity questions, check the targets before the tests: a recovery target looser than the business can bear fails even when it is met.

questions.subtopic: 2A3 Planning around key risks and controls. An owner's share money booked as a loan
questions.question: Planning assurance on a Namibian fishing company's covenant, debt no greater than equity, auditor Tuyeni learns an owner's cash, paid for ordinary shares, was booked as a loan payable. How is the cash BEST classed?

options.A: A loan payable, since it is owed to the owner on request
options.B: A current liability, since it is owed within the year
options.C: Retained earnings, since it is kept in the business
options.D: Contributed capital, since it adds to the owners' stake

questions.key_concept: Cash owners pay in for an ownership stake is contributed capital, part of equity; only amounts owed to creditors are liabilities.
questions.pre_read: Recall how equity and liabilities differ, and where cash paid in by owners for shares belongs on a balance sheet.
questions.correct_explanation: OpenStax's accounting text treats what owners invest for a share of ownership as equity, with contributed capital holding what they pay in, apart from retained earnings, the profits kept; liabilities are amounts owed to creditors. Cash paid for ordinary shares is contributed capital, so booking it as a loan overstates debt and understates equity, and the covenant looks weaker than it is. Option A treats the owner as a lender.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: cash an owner lends on repayment terms is a loan payable, but cash paid for ordinary shares buys ownership and is owed back to no one.
wrong_explanations.B: A current liability is owed to a creditor within about a year; cash that bought shares creates no debt at all, current or long-term.
wrong_explanations.C: Retained earnings holds the profits kept in the business; cash that owners pay in for shares is contributed capital, a separate part of equity.

tips: Eliminate: B, because cash paid for shares creates no debt, current or long-term, and C, because retained earnings holds profits kept, not amounts owners pay in.
Final two: D beats A because cash paid for ordinary shares buys ownership and sits in equity; only cash an owner lends on repayment terms is a loan payable.
Exam cue: on CIA planning questions, ask what the provider of funds received: an ownership stake makes equity, a promise of repayment makes a liability.

questions.subtopic: 2A3 Planning around key risks and controls. Developers releasing their own code
questions.question: Sigrun, an internal auditor scoping an Icelandic insurer's claims system, learns developers move their own code into production; change tickets record no approver. Which risk MOST needs rating?

options.A: Developers' production access could expose claimants' medical records
options.B: Changes no one else approved could alter how claims are paid
options.C: Claim amounts keyed in error could pass without input checks
options.D: Claims could be paid without a claims manager's approval

questions.key_concept: Proposed system changes are reviewed and approved before release, and duties are split so one person cannot both make and release a change unchecked.
questions.pre_read: Recall what change control and separation of duties require before code reaches production, and what can go wrong without them.
questions.correct_explanation: NIST SP 800-53 has proposed system changes reviewed and approved or rejected, with each decision recorded, before release, and splits duties so one person cannot misuse a privilege unchecked. Developers releasing their own unapproved code can change how claims are paid, by mistake or on purpose, so Standard 13.2 has Sigrun rate that risk, fraud included. Option A is a real access concern, but the stem's facts concern changes.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: developer access to live data is a confidentiality risk, but the stem's facts are developers releasing their own code with no approver, a change control gap.
wrong_explanations.C: Input checks catch keying errors in claims; the stem says nothing about how claims are keyed, and its gap lies in how system changes are released.
wrong_explanations.D: A missing claims approval is a payment control gap, but the stem's missing approver is on change tickets, which govern changes to the system itself.

tips: Eliminate: C, because the stem says nothing about how claims are keyed, and D, because the missing approver is on change tickets, not on claim payments.
Final two: B beats A because code its own developer releases unapproved can rewrite how every claim is paid; reviewed, approved and separated changes are what the stem shows missing.
Exam cue: on CIA planning questions, when one person writes and releases system changes with no approval, rate the risk of unauthorized changes to processing.

questions.subtopic: 2A4 Choosing the engagement approach. Hours with no breakdown behind them
questions.question: Supervisor Leilani's plan for a Samoan airline's fuel engagement gives three objectives total hours and a reporting date; the chief audit executive asks when each objective's fieldwork ends. What should Leilani do FIRST?

options.A: Break each objective into tasks, then estimate each one's hours
options.B: Set each objective's end date by spreading its hours evenly across weeks
options.C: Re-estimate each objective's hours from last year, then set its dates
options.D: Ask the chief audit executive to move the reporting date later

questions.key_concept: A work breakdown structure splits the work into tasks small enough to estimate and order; the schedule is then built from those tasks.
questions.pre_read: Recall the order of project planning steps: breaking the work down, estimating and sequencing it, then setting dates.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 13.6 requires the work program to name the tasks each objective needs, and Standard 13.5's considerations have staff and time assigned by those steps. OpenStax's information systems text orders the work the same way: a work breakdown structure of smaller tasks, then estimates and sequence, then a schedule. End dates spread from a lump of hours, as in option B, rest on no estimate of the work.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: a schedule answers the chief audit executive, but dates come after the work is broken into tasks and each is estimated and sequenced.
wrong_explanations.C: Last year's hours can inform task estimates, but a fresh total per objective is still a lump; dates set from it have no tasks behind them.
wrong_explanations.D: Moving the reporting date fits a plan shown to be unachievable; nothing here shows the date cannot be met, only that the work is not broken down.

tips: Eliminate: C, because a total taken from last year is still a lump with no tasks behind it, and D, because nothing shows the reporting date cannot be met.
Final two: A beats B because a schedule is built from estimated tasks; dates spread from a lump of hours cannot show when each objective's work will really end.
Exam cue: on CIA project management questions, break the work down before scheduling it: tasks first, then estimates and order, then dates.

questions.subtopic: 2A1 Engagement objectives and scope. A subcontractor inside the vendor's contract
questions.question: Planning third-party assurance at a Peruvian insurer, auditor Milagros learns its claims processor, as the insurer's contract allows, passes claimants' bank details to a smaller firm for keying. How should Milagros BEST treat that firm?

options.A: Exclude it, as the insurer signed no contract with the firm
options.B: Include it, as subcontracted work within the processor's contract
options.C: Include it once a right-to-audit clause is shown to reach it
options.D: Exclude it until management records the firm in its vendor listing

questions.key_concept: The Third-Party Topical Requirement reaches subcontractors a vendor's contract allows; a missing audit clause may limit evidence, but it does not limit that reach.
questions.pre_read: Recall how far down a vendor's chain the Third-Party Topical Requirement reaches, and what a missing right-to-audit clause changes.
questions.correct_explanation: The Third-Party Topical Requirement covers subcontracted relationships that a third party's contract allows, fourth parties and beyond, and asks internal auditors to prioritize them by risk; a firm keying claimants' bank details ranks high. Option C ties the firm's place in scope to a right-to-audit clause. The user guide says a missing clause may limit the assurance internal audit obtains; access then refused is a Standard 13.3 scope limitation, discussed with management.

wrong_explanations.A: The requirement does not stop at contracts the insurer signed: it reaches subcontractors that a vendor's contract allows, which is this firm's position.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: a missing audit clause may limit the evidence; access then refused is a scope limitation to discuss with management, not a reason to drop the firm.
wrong_explanations.D: A complete listing of third-party relationships is a control the requirement has internal auditors assess; a gap in it may be a finding, not a gate on the scope.

tips: Eliminate: A, because the requirement reaches subcontractors a vendor's contract allows, and D, because the vendor listing is a control to assess, not a gate on the scope.

Final two: B beats C because a missing right-to-audit clause may limit evidence, and any access then refused is a scope limitation for management; it does not take an allowed subcontractor out of scope.
Exam cue: on CIA third-party questions, follow the organization's data down the vendor's chain; who signed the contract does not set the engagement's reach.

questions.subtopic: 2A3 Planning around key risks and controls. A high-risk vendor after its contract ends
questions.question: A Ghanaian bank ended its contract with a payroll bureau, one of its highest-risk vendors, in March and moved payroll in-house. Planning June's third-party assurance, how should auditor Akosua BEST treat the bureau?

options.A: Assess how the bank vetted the bureau before first selecting it
options.B: Exclude the bureau, recording the contract's March end as the reason
options.C: Assess the bank's exit steps: access revoked, staff data returned or destroyed
options.D: Assess how the bank monitored the bureau's staff-data security terms until March

questions.key_concept: The third-party life cycle ends with offboarding: for vendors prioritized by risk, auditors assess management's exit steps, access revoked and data returned or destroyed.
questions.pre_read: Place the vendor in its relationship with the bank today before deciding whether, and how, the engagement covers it.
questions.correct_explanation: For third parties prioritized by risk, the Third-Party Topical Requirement has internal auditors assess management's formal offboarding plan, which revokes access and returns or destroys the organization's data, and consider every life cycle stage. A payroll bureau that held staff data is at that exit stage, so Akosua plans to assess the bank's exit steps. Option B treats the contract's end as a reason to exclude, yet that is when offboarding begins.

wrong_explanations.A: Due diligence at selection is a real control, but it bears on choosing a vendor; for a relationship that has ended, the exit holds the live risk.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: an exclusion with a recorded reason is allowed, but a contract's end opens the offboarding stage the requirement covers; data and access can outlast the contract.
wrong_explanations.D: Monitoring is a real control for prioritized vendors, but checks made until March test contract performance; they cannot show whether the bureau still holds staff data or access.

tips: Eliminate: A, because selection checks bear on choosing a vendor, not on one that has left, and D, because monitoring tests performance under the contract, not where staff data and access sit after it.
Final two: C beats B because offboarding is a life cycle stage the requirement covers for vendors prioritized by risk; a contract's end begins that stage rather than closing it.
Exam cue: on CIA third-party questions, a relationship ends at offboarding, not on the contract's end date; ask where the organization's data and access still sit.

questions.subtopic: 2A5 Detailed engagement risk assessment. Billing risks a contract says the vendor owns
questions.question: For assurance on a Jordanian utility's outsourced billing, auditor Rania finds management's risk register omits billing risks, saying the contract makes the billing firm own them. How should Rania's engagement risk assessment BEST treat them?

options.A: Rank them as the firm's risks, reviewed through its assurance report
options.B: Rank them as shared risks, split by the contract's terms
options.C: Rank them as the utility's, rated low for the contract's penalty clauses
options.D: Rank them as the utility's risks, with the contract as one response

questions.key_concept: An organization using a third party stays accountable for the risks to its objectives; a contract is a response to assess, not a new owner.
questions.pre_read: Recall who the Third-Party Topical Requirement holds accountable for risks when a third party does the work, and what Standard 13.2 asks.
questions.correct_explanation: Under the Third-Party Topical Requirement, engaging a vendor hands over work, not accountability: the utility still answers for risks to its billing objectives, and they still have to be found, weighed and managed. Standard 13.2 has Rania identify and rank significant risks and their intended controls, so the billing risks stay the utility's and the contract is one response to assess. Option A keeps the risks in view, but as the firm's.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: it keeps the risks in view, but as the firm's; the utility stays accountable, and the firm's report needs its reliability checked before any reliance.
wrong_explanations.B: Sharing is a risk response, not a split of accountability: the requirement keeps accountability with the organization that engaged the firm, so Rania ranks them in full as the utility's.
wrong_explanations.C: Penalty clauses share the cost of a failure, one response, but service, regulatory and reputational harm stays with the utility, so the clauses cannot set the rating.

tips: Eliminate: B, because sharing is a response, not a split of accountability, and C, because penalty clauses share a failure's cost, not its effect on the utility's objectives.
Final two: D beats A because the requirement keeps accountability with the organization that engaged the firm; the risks are the utility's, and the contract is a response to assess, not a new owner.
Exam cue: on CIA third-party questions, outsourcing moves the work, not the accountability; rank the risk where the organization's objectives sit.

questions.subtopic: 2A5 Detailed engagement risk assessment. Clear messages with no check on how staff take them
questions.question: Planning organizational behavior assurance at a Scottish whisky distiller, auditor Morag finds leaders' town halls and videos state clear, consistent expectations; the one staff survey covers pay. How is the tone control's design BEST rated?

options.A: Incomplete: nothing checks that staff understand and support them
options.B: Sound: clear, consistent expectations reach staff through accessible channels
options.C: Incomplete: the expectations need a yearly training course behind them
options.D: Sound, provided site managers repeat the expectations at shift briefings

questions.key_concept: Tone at the top runs both ways: leaders' expectations go out, and a planned feedback route shows whether staff grasp and accept them.
questions.pre_read: Recall what the Organizational Behavior Topical Requirement has internal auditors assess in the controls that set and spread expected behavior.
questions.correct_explanation: Under the Organizational Behavior Topical Requirement, the tone control has a sending side and a listening side, and internal auditors assess both. Morag's facts show only the sending side: steady, clear messages from leaders. A survey about pay cannot tell management whether staff took the messages in or agree with them, so the design has a gap. Option B rates the sending side as if it were the whole control.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: clear messages through accessible channels are half the control; the requirement also expects feedback showing staff grasp and accept them, which a pay survey cannot give.
wrong_explanations.C: Training is a separate control under the requirement; a course would not show how staff read leaders' messages, so the tone control's own gap would stay open.
wrong_explanations.D: Site managers repeating the messages helps them reach every level, but it is still sending; only feedback from staff shows whether they grasp and accept them.

tips: Eliminate: C, because training is its own control and would not show how staff read the messages, and D, because repeating the messages down the line is still sending, not hearing back.
Final two: A beats B because the requirement's tone control includes structured feedback on whether staff understand and support the expectations; sending clear messages is only the first half.
Exam cue: on CIA culture questions, tone at the top is judged at the receiving end too; ask what tells leaders how staff heard the message.

questions.subtopic: 2A5 Detailed engagement risk assessment. A committee that never questions a loan
questions.question: Planning credit assurance at a Bangladeshi microfinance lender, with organizational behavior in scope, auditor Nasrin reads a year's committee minutes and observes two meetings: loans within limits, approved unanimously, unquestioned. Which risk MOST needs rating?

options.A: Members' interests in borrowers go undeclared before each vote
options.B: Members back every proposal without testing its weaknesses
options.C: Minutes too thin to show how each approval was reached
options.D: Approval limits set above the board's tolerance for credit losses

questions.key_concept: Decisions made without effective challenge are one of the user guide's example behavioral risk indicators, even when every approval meets its limits.
questions.pre_read: Recall which signs of group behavior the Organizational Behavior user guide treats as indicators of behavioral risk.
questions.correct_explanation: The Organizational Behavior user guide gives decisions made without effective challenge, or without other views, as an example of a behavioral risk indicator, and the requirement has internal auditors assess whether behavior is monitored. A year of unanimous, unquestioned approvals, matched in the meetings Nasrin observes, is that pattern: a risk to loan quality that compliance with limits cannot reveal, so Standard 13.2 has it rated. Option C reads the pattern as a records gap.

wrong_explanations.A: Undeclared interests are a conflict the requirement names, but nothing here links any member to a borrower; the stem's pattern is the whole committee's silence.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: thin minutes may be part of the picture, but the meetings Nasrin watched match them; unanimous, unquestioned votes signal missing challenge, a risk to loan quality.
wrong_explanations.D: Limits above tolerance would be a risk appetite gap, but nothing says these limits are wrong; loans meeting them do not show how they were decided.

tips: Eliminate: A, because nothing links any member to a borrower, and D, because nothing suggests the limits exceed the board's tolerance; loans within limits say nothing about how they were decided.
Final two: B beats C because the meetings match the minutes, and the user guide gives decisions without effective challenge as a behavioral risk indicator; the pattern is how the group decides.
Exam cue: on CIA culture questions, a group that never disagrees is a behavior signal; controls that all pass can still sit on decisions nobody tests.

questions.subtopic: 2A5 Detailed engagement risk assessment. One shortcut, thirty separate warnings
questions.question: Planning organizational behavior assurance at a Peruvian zinc mine, auditor Killa finds 30 fitters warned this year, one warning each, for skipping conveyor lockout checks; each warning closed the case. Which risk MOST needs rating?

options.A: Warnings too mild to stop other fitters skipping the checks
options.B: Fitters hired without any check of their safety attitudes
options.C: A shortcut fitters share, whose cause no one traces or corrects
options.D: Lockout checks missing from the written maintenance procedure

questions.key_concept: The same lapse by many people is a behavioral pattern, the way work is done; handling each case alone leaves its cause in place.
questions.pre_read: Recall what the Organizational Behavior Topical Requirement has internal auditors assess in how an organization manages behavior issues.
questions.correct_explanation: The Organizational Behavior Topical Requirement has internal auditors assess whether the organization can spot and correct patterns of behavior, and its user guide sets patterns, the way things are done, against one-off events. Thirty fitters taking one shortcut is a pattern, yet each case closed alone, so whatever drives it stays untouched; Standard 13.2 has Killa rate that risk. Option A also treats the cases one at a time.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: lenient discipline can fail to deter, but harsher warnings would still treat thirty cases one by one; nothing would find why so many fitters take the shortcut.
wrong_explanations.B: Hiring checks on behavior are a real control, but nothing ties the shortcut to recent hires; thirty fitters over a year point to how the work is done.
wrong_explanations.D: Fitters were warned for skipping the checks, so the procedure already requires them; the gap lies in practice, not in the written steps.

tips: Eliminate: B, because nothing ties the shortcut to how fitters were hired, and D, because the warnings show the procedure already requires the checks.
Final two: C beats A; mild discipline can fail to deter, but the requirement looks for patterns and their correction, and harsher warnings would still handle each case alone.
Exam cue: on CIA culture questions, the same lapse by many people is a pattern; ask what in the setting drives it before rating the individuals.
